anglican.sola_scriptura:
Anglicans hold that Holy Scripture contains all things necessary for salvation, and that nothing which is not read in it or proved by it may be required as an article of faith. This is stated in the Thirty-Nine Articles. Scripture is therefore the primary and decisive authority in the church.

Anglicans do not, however, set Scripture against the church's tradition. They read the Bible in the light of the ancient creeds and the teaching of the early church, and they use reason to understand and apply it. This is often summarized as Scripture, tradition and reason, and is associated with the teacher Richard Hooker. Anglicans emphasize these three differently. Evangelical Anglicans stress Scripture most strongly, and Anglo-Catholics stress tradition, and both would say Scripture has the final word.
anglican.apocrypha:
Anglicans include the Apocrypha, the books also called deuterocanonical, in the Bible and read them in worship, and yet they do not use them to establish doctrine. Article Six of the Thirty-Nine Articles says that the church reads them for example of life and instruction of manners, but does not apply them to establish any doctrine.

This follows the practice of Jerome, who separated these books from those in the Hebrew canon. Anglican lectionaries include readings from the Apocrypha, and many Anglican Bibles print them in a separate section. Anglicans thus stand between traditions that treat these books as fully canonical Scripture and those that leave them out of the Bible entirely. Individual Anglicans give them more or less weight.
anglican.tradition:
Anglicans value the tradition of the church as a faithful guide to Scripture, especially the creeds, the worship of the early church and the teaching of the Fathers. They understand their church as both catholic and reformed: part of the ancient church of the West, and shaped by the Reformation.

The Book of Common Prayer is one of the main carriers of this tradition. Tradition is respected but is judged by Scripture, so that a custom which contradicts the Bible can be reformed. Anglicans differ about how much weight tradition should carry. Anglo-Catholics look to it more fully, and Evangelical Anglicans treat it more cautiously, but both take part in the same church and pray from the same prayer book tradition.
anglican.apostolic_succession:
Anglicans have kept the historic episcopate, meaning that their bishops are consecrated in a line of succession going back to the apostles through the laying on of hands. It is one of the four points of the Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral, along with Scripture, the creeds and the two sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

Anglicans do not all understand its meaning in the same way. Anglo-Catholics regard it as essential to a valid ministry and sacraments. Many Evangelical Anglicans value it as a sign of the church's continuity and unity, and of faithfulness to apostolic teaching, but do not treat it as required for a church to be a true church. The Anglican Communion has generally not denied that other churches have real ministries.
anglican.polity:
Anglican churches are governed by an episcopal polity: bishops have oversight of dioceses, and the church is led by bishops together with clergy and laity. Most Anglican provinces have synods with houses of bishops, clergy and laity, where decisions about doctrine, worship and order are made together.

Each national or regional church is self-governing, and together they form the Anglican Communion, a fellowship of churches which are in communion with the Archbishop of Canterbury. He is a focus of unity and is honored as first among equals, but he does not rule the other provinces. This makes the Communion less centralized than the Roman Catholic Church, and more united by shared heritage, prayer and relationships than by a single authority.
anglican.episcopacy:
In Anglican churches a bishop is the chief pastor of a diocese. He or she teaches the faith, ordains priests and deacons, confirms, and oversees the clergy and the mission of the church in the diocese. Bishops are consecrated by other bishops, in a way that links the church to the apostolic ministry, and they are usually elected with the participation of clergy and laity.

Anglicans regard the episcopate as an ancient and valuable order which the church has kept, and which serves unity. Many Anglican provinces now have women bishops, though some provinces and members do not accept this. Anglicans differ on how essential bishops are, but all Anglican churches retain them as part of their identity.
anglican.confirmation:
In Anglican churches, confirmation is the rite in which a baptized person, guided by the bishop, publicly reaffirms the promises of baptism and receives the bishop's prayer and the laying on of hands for the strengthening of the Holy Spirit. It is usually for those who are old enough to make their own profession of faith.

Anglican teaching distinguishes the two sacraments given by Christ in the gospel, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, from other rites. Anglo-Catholics count confirmation among seven sacraments, while others regard it as a rite of the church. In earlier times it was required before receiving communion, though many Anglican provinces now admit baptized children to communion before confirmation. Confirmation is also the way that people from other traditions are often received into the church.
anglican.confession:
Anglicans practice both a general confession, said together in worship, and private confession to a priest. The private practice is often summarized by the saying that all may, none must, some should. It is available to anyone who wishes to make their confession and receive absolution, but it is not required of anyone.

The priest hears the confession under a strict seal of secrecy, and pronounces God's forgiveness. Anglo-Catholics make regular use of it, and it is more familiar there. Many Evangelical Anglicans confess directly to God and to one another, and use private confession little or not at all. Both are viewed as legitimate ways within the tradition of receiving God's forgiveness.
anglican.holy_orders:
Anglicans understand the ordained ministry as consisting of three orders: bishops, priests and deacons. Persons are ordained to these orders by the prayer of the church and the laying on of hands by a bishop, following the rites of the Ordinal in the Book of Common Prayer or its successors.

The church holds that God calls people to this ministry and that the church tests and affirms the call. Anglo-Catholics understand Holy Orders as a sacrament, while others regard it as an ancient order of ministry without calling it a sacrament of the gospel. Women are ordained as priests and deacons in many Anglican provinces, and as bishops in a number of them, although some provinces and members do not accept this development.
anglican.liturgy:
Anglican worship is shaped by the Book of Common Prayer, first issued in the sixteenth century and revised many times, together with later prayer books in many provinces. Its services include daily Morning and Evening Prayer, and Holy Communion, and they are meant to be prayed together in the language of the people.

The idea of common prayer is that the whole church prays with one voice, using set forms so that Scripture, the Psalms and the creeds shape the faith of ordinary worshippers. Anglican worship ranges widely, from formal and ceremonial services to simpler and more informal ones, but the prayer book heritage usually gives it a shared structure. Many Anglicans see the liturgy as teaching the faith as much as the sermon does.
anglican.liturgical_calendar:
Anglicans keep the church year: Advent, Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, along with holy days that commemorate saints and other events. The year is structured by a lectionary which takes the congregation through much of the Bible over time.

The church year is understood as a way of walking through the life of Christ and of keeping the gospel central in the rhythm of worship. Anglicans also commemorate saints, though the degree of emphasis differs. Anglo-Catholics keep many feasts, and more Evangelical parishes may keep only the major seasons. In all cases, the calendar is a way of marking time by the story of salvation.
anglican.sign_of_the_cross:
In Anglican churches the sign of the cross is used in baptism, when the newly baptized person is signed with the cross as a mark of belonging to Christ, and by many worshippers at the blessing, the creed and other points in the service. It is a way of confessing faith in the Trinity and in the cross of Christ.

Its use is a matter of custom and freedom. Anglo-Catholics and many others make the sign of the cross frequently, and many Evangelical Anglicans do not. The Book of Common Prayer's baptismal service includes the signing with the cross, and no Anglican church forbids the practice. It is understood as a gesture of devotion and not as having power in itself.
anglican.rosary:
Some Anglicans use Anglican prayer beads, a set of beads modeled loosely on the rosary but with a different structure, which are used for meditation, for the Jesus Prayer, for Psalms and for intercessory prayer. The beads help focus the mind and give a rhythm to prayer.

Some Anglo-Catholics also pray the traditional Rosary, with its prayers and meditations on the life of Christ and Mary. Use of either is a matter of personal devotion and is not required. Many Anglicans, particularly Evangelicals, do not use beads at all, and some are uneasy about devotion to Mary. Where they are used, the beads are understood as an aid to prayer rather than as something that has power in itself.
anglican.purgatory:
The Thirty-Nine Articles reject the Roman doctrine of purgatory, as it was taught at the time of the Reformation, as having no warrant in Scripture. Anglicans speak instead of the intermediate state, the condition of the faithful departed between death and the resurrection, held in the care of God.

Modern Anglicans differ. Many simply commit the departed to God's mercy and speak of rest and growth in his presence. Some, especially Anglo-Catholics, pray for the dead and are open to the idea of cleansing or growth after death without adopting every part of the Catholic teaching. Others avoid prayers for the dead altogether. What Anglicans generally agree on is hope in the resurrection and in God's care for those who have died.
